I came across this on Substack. Wondering what STRL will have or say : “US midterms impact on AI infra stocks:

Not simply good or bad for AI. It changes winners and losers!

First, three interesting facts:

1) Texas just elected a Democratic governor for the first time since the 1990s, and she wants a MORATORIUM on new data centers, an end to their tax breaks, and developers paying their full electricity costs.

2) Wells Fargo: 27% (!!) of planned US data center gigawatts are in Texas.

3) 33 local measures restricting data centers passed or are leading. Only ONE pro-build measure won (North Dakota). 56% of voters called data centers a crucial or major factor.

Impact:

1) Capacity that is already POWERED and PERMITTED just got pricing power. Insanely good for companies like $NBIS that have 0 Texas exposure and instead build globally across Europe, the Middle East and Asia! Some reports say Anthropic uses up to 75% of its compute for training. OpenAI is probably similar. That can be done ANYWHERE! So scarcity here will not lower demand, but it will massively lower supply. This significantly improves the already great economics.

2) Operators sitting on stranded or delayed power are obviously giga screwed! This will lead to many delays and straight-up project cancellations. Good for the ones who can deliver, horrible for the others. Some won't survive.

3) On-site power gets (even) MORE valuable when the grid is the bottleneck. Very bullish $BE $FCEL 🚀

Yet overnight $CRWV fell 7%, $NBIS 4% and $ORCL 4%, as if they were all the same 👀

The situation is still this: whoever can deliver will crush it. The rest will get crushed.”

A quick search ;

Sterling Infrastructure (STRL) does **not publicly disclose an exact number of Texas data-center projects**. The best supported public figure is that it is doing **both construction and electrical work on two data-center campuses** in Texas, while management describes additional Texas opportunities in West Texas and North Central Texas that have not yet been fully quantified.[1][2]

## What is publicly known

- Sterling acquired Texas-based electrical contractor CEC Facilities Group in 2025, enabling it to combine site development/civil work with electrical services for data centers.[1]
- A company-related report states Sterling has already performed **both construction and electrical work for two data-center campuses**.[1]
- On its Q3 2026 earnings call, management said it is active on Texas projects and that CEC has “second phases,” with further work emerging in **West Texas** and **North Central Texas**—but it did not give a project count.[2][3]
- Management also said Texas demand exceeds Sterling’s current capacity and that Texas should be its largest data-center state over the next five years.[4][5]

## Bottom line

| Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| Exact disclosed Texas data-center project count? | **Not disclosed** |
| Publicly identifiable campuses with combined civil + electrical scope? | **2** [1] |
| Additional Texas projects referenced? | Yes—multiple phased projects/campuses in West Texas and North Central Texas, but no count given. [2][3] |

So, if you mean **confirmed, separately identifiable Texas data-center campuses**, the public evidence points to **two**; if you mean **all current and prospective Texas engagements**, Sterling has not disclosed a total.[1][2]

Fast answer from perplexity

SNEX has fallen sharply—roughly 11% over one month, 22% over three months, and about 42% year-to-date as of mid-October 2026—despite strong reported revenue and net-income growth. The decline appears driven mainly by earnings-quality concerns, weaker retail/FX results, insider selling, and a reassessment of its valuation.[1][2][3]

## Main reasons

| Driver | What happened | Why it pressured the stock |
|---|---|---|
| **Earnings expectations mismatch** | Q3 FY2026 adjusted diluted EPS was $1.00, below some analysts’ $1.23 forecast, even though revenue grew 47% year over year to $719.7 million and net income more than doubled. [4][2] | Investors focused on the shortfall versus expectations rather than the strong headline growth. [2][3] |
| **Softer retail and FX results** | Self-Directed Retail revenue fell 20% and segment income fell 39%; FX and CFD revenue fell 19% year over year. [4] | These businesses are sensitive to trading volatility and client activity, so their weakness raised concerns about earnings momentum. [4] |
| **Valuation reset** | The stock had traded as high as $94.66 over the prior 52 weeks; by mid-October it was around $57–$60. [1][5] | After a large run-up, investors appear to have reduced the premium they were willing to pay, particularly as growth became more mixed. [1][6] |
| **Insider selling** | The CEO sold 45,000 shares for about $2.68 million under a pre-arranged 10b5-1 plan; an executive vice-chairman also sold 76,148 shares for about $4.6 million. Reports cited roughly $51.6 million of insider sales over 90 days. [7][6][5] | Insider selling is not automatically negative, especially when preplanned, but the scale and timing added to bearish sentiment. [6][5] |
| **Analyst sentiment shifted** | Several firms moved SNEX toward Hold, and the consensus rating reportedly became Hold. [6] | Downgrades or more cautious ratings can trigger selling even when a company’s fundamentals remain solid. [6] |
| **Rising short interest** | Short interest was reported at 4.8 million shares, or 4.4% of float, up 180% since October 2025. [8] | More investors positioning for a decline can amplify downward moves. [8] |

## Important nuance

The underlying quarter was not weak in absolute terms: StoneX reported record trailing-twelve-month net income of $526.9 million, up 77%, with an 18.4% quarterly return on equity.  The issue was therefore less “bad results” and more that investors had priced in stronger earnings per share, while parts of the business—especially retail trading and FX/CFDs—showed clear softness.[2][4]

## What to watch next

- **Q4 FY2026 results:** whether retail, FX/CFD, and payments trends stabilize or improve.[4]
- **Volatility conditions:** StoneX’s trading and hedging businesses can benefit from volatility, but the company noted moderation during the latest quarter.[4]
- **Insider filings:** whether sales remain routine/preplanned or become broader and more discretionary.[5][7]
- **Valuation versus earnings quality:** the stock’s fall may reflect multiple compression rather than a collapse in operating performance.[1][2]

This is market-context information, not personalized investment advice; SNEX’s earnings are inherently sensitive to trading volumes, commodity markets, volatility, and interest-rate conditions.[4]

comment.body:
Hi Ben,

I don’t have any thresholds but when my model shows me more than 2x the market (eg RYAM) I don’t invest until I figure out what the market is pricing. 
I would enter the consensus estimates in the model and see what price the model gives you. (The dcf tool on RankedStocks.com has the consensus estimates prepopulated). If still the model is materially higher than the current stock price then your model has something mechanically wrong (like a frozen formula).  If the model gives you something closer to current market price then you know it is the assumptions. 

At that stage try to understand why the market assumptions differs from yours (channel checks are great for this). 

If not many analysts follow the company and channel checks are difficult, I would suggest talking to IR and challenge your assumptions, many companies would not give you estimates that are not public but they would at least tell you if you are way off. One time I had a company that even told me to send my model and sent me feedback afterwards!

I know when the entire AI market is down so much on investor sentiment, you may 'feel' like trimming, but I think this is the wrong move. The CLS earnings results show that there is still strong demand and remember everything AI related need memory.

One new dimension. In a recent All-In podcast episode, they were discussing the rise of open-source models. The way Anthropic handled Fable and discriminated who can use it, plus reports that Anthropic and OpenAI are using whatever you input in the model for their own product development (think what happened to Figma). So their is new demand for open-source models. The software likely will be based on the Chinese open-source models. But hardware will come fron NVDA and AMD (the latter released a chip just for that!). That hardware comes with memory and I think more people/corporations using open-source means incremental memory demand (economies of de-scale).
